The estimate above is a rule of thumb, not a law — the true count depends on the exact chopping, and other languages fare differently (many need more tokens per word than English, one reason the same conversation can be "longer" to a model in another language). But for planning — how much text fits, why a huge document got cut off, why a bill scales with a long chat — three-quarters of a word per token will steer you right.
I asked an AI the same question twice and got two different answers. Is it broken, or is that normal?

Normal — and understanding why tells you something real about how these systems work.

**The mechanism: choosing, not looking up.** The model doesn't retrieve a stored answer; it *constructs* one, piece by piece. At each step, several next pieces are plausible, with different likelihoods — one phrasing at 40%, another at 25%, others trailing off. Most systems deliberately *sample*: they pick among the likely options with weighted randomness rather than always taking the single most likely. So the answer is written by a process with dice in it — loaded dice, favoring good continuations, but dice. Ask twice and the early choices differ; once the first sentences diverge, the rest follows the path taken, and you get two genuinely different performances of an answer.

**The analogy.** It's asking the same storyteller to tell the same story on two evenings. The facts and the teller are the same; the telling is improvised each time, and no two performances match word for word. A search engine, by contrast, is a librarian: ask twice, get the same shelf pointed out — which is why AI answers *feel* alive and search results feel stable.

**Where it matters practically.** The variation is a dial, not a defect: systems can be set to near-zero randomness for tasks needing consistency (and even then, tiny differences in conditions can flip a close call between two near-equal options). For you, the useful habits are: don't treat a single answer as *the* answer — for anything important, asking again and comparing is a legitimate check, since two runs agreeing on the facts is weak evidence they're anchored, and disagreeing is a loud warning. And when an answer seems off, "try again" isn't superstition — it's re-rolling a process that was never deterministic in the first place.
What's the actual difference between asking a search engine and asking an AI chatbot? They both answer questions.

They do opposite jobs that happen to share a costume. A search engine *finds*; a chatbot *composes*.

**The search engine** maintains an enormous index of the web — pages it has visited and catalogued. Your question is matched against the index, and it returns *pointers*: links to pages that exist, written by identifiable people and organizations, which you then read and judge. It invents nothing. Its answers are exactly as good as the pages it finds, and you can inspect the source yourself.

**The chatbot** has no shelf to point at. It generates a fresh answer, word by word, from patterns learned in training. What it says may never have been written anywhere before — which is the source of both its magic (it can synthesize, rephrase, adapt to your exact question and level) and its characteristic failure: it can produce fluent statements with no source at all, including invented ones, delivered in the same tone as the solid ones.

**Where the contrast teaches the usage.** Each fails in its own direction. Search fails by finding nothing, or by surfacing confident rubbish that a human published — but the rubbish has an address, and you can evaluate who's speaking. Chatbots fail by composing nonsense that *sounds* sourced. So the working division: use search when the fact must be verifiable and the source matters (news, official information, anything you'll act on); use the chatbot when the work is transformation — explaining, summarizing something you've provided, drafting, brainstorming, translating a hard text into a plain one. Increasingly the two are being bolted together — chatbots that search first and cite what they found — which is an admission from the builders themselves: generation is a fine writer and a careless librarian, so they've hired it a librarian.
Where does an AI's knowledge actually come from? Does it have a giant library inside that it looks things up in?

It learned from a giant library, but it doesn't keep one inside. The distinction between *learning from* and *looking up in* is the key to the model's strangest behaviors.

**Training as digestion, not storage.** During training, the model processed vast collections of text — books, articles, websites, code — and adjusted its internal numbers to capture the patterns. What remains is not the texts but the *imprint* of the texts: something closer to what a widely read person carries in their head than to a filing cabinet. A scholar who has read ten thousand books can't produce most of them verbatim, can't tell you which page a fact came from, and will occasionally misremember — while genuinely *knowing* a tremendous amount, in the sense of being able to reason with it, summarize it, and connect it. The model is like that, at inhuman scale and without the human's judgment about what's solid.

**Where the analogy explains the symptoms.** *Why it paraphrases well but quotes badly:* gist survives digestion; exact wording mostly doesn't — so long quotations and precise citations are exactly where errors creep in. *Why it can be out of date:* the imprint ends when training ended; the world after that date isn't in it unless the product fetches fresh information live. *Why it can't show its sources:* there are no sources in the cabinet to open — the pattern doesn't retain which texts taught it what, so when it offers a citation, that citation is itself generated text, shaped like a citation, and it can be fabricated as fluently as anything else.

**The honest summary.** The model's knowledge is real but *unindexed*: a vast, compressed, sourceless sense of how things are described. That is a genuinely new kind of knowing, and its failure modes — confident, fluent, occasionally invented — are precisely the ones you'd predict from knowledge stored as imprint rather than as records.
What is 'fine-tuning'? I hear companies fine-tune a model for their industry. Does that mean teaching it new facts?

Fine-tuning is extra training, done after the main training, on a narrower set of examples — and it's better at teaching *behavior* than *facts*.

**The analogy.** Take a broadly educated graduate and give them a season working in one particular kitchen. They won't forget their education; they'll absorb the house style — how this kitchen plates, what it calls things, which shortcuts are acceptable, the rhythm of the work. Fine-tuning does that to a model: continuing its education on examples from one company, task, or style, so its predictions lean toward that house's way of doing things.

**What it changes well.** Voice and format (answers shaped like your company's support replies), task skills (classifying your documents your way, writing in your templates), and judgment calls at the margins (which of two plausible answers this house prefers). These are pattern-level things, and patterns are what training adjusts.

**Where the analogy breaks — the fact problem.** Owners often hope fine-tuning will *install* their facts: the product catalogue, the policy manual. It's a poor filing cabinet for that. Facts woven in by training become part of the imprint — unindexed, unverifiable, prone to being paraphrased wrong or blended with similar facts — and updating them means retraining. For facts, the reliable architecture is the opposite: keep the model general, and *hand it the documents at question time* (the context mechanism), so it answers from pages it can see and you can correct. The working rule: fine-tune for how it should behave; supply documents for what it should know. Companies that grasp the difference build systems that are both personable and accurate; companies that don't build a model that speaks in their voice while confidently misremembering their prices.
How does an AI create an image from a sentence? Is it searching for a photo that matches, or collaging existing pictures?

Neither — and the actual method is stranger than both. In broad terms, the dominant kind of image AI (a diffusion model) *sculpts from noise*.

**The process.** Training showed the model millions of images paired with descriptions, while it practiced a peculiar skill: taking a picture corrupted by static and learning to remove a little of the static, guided by the description. At generation time, it starts from a screen of pure random noise — television static — and repeatedly refines it, step by step, each pass making the image slightly more coherent and slightly more like the description: shapes emerge, then objects, then details. It's less like photography and more like watching a figure condense out of fog, under the constant instruction of your sentence.

**Why it's not a collage or a search.** Nothing is retrieved and nothing is pasted; the pixels are manufactured fresh by the refinement process. That's why it can depict things that have never existed — a teapot shaped like a lighthouse — and why the same prompt yields a different image each time: the starting noise is random, and different static condenses into different pictures.

**Where the picture needs audits — the famous glitches explained.** Hands with the wrong number of fingers and garbled text in images aren't random malfunctions; they follow from the method. The model shapes *appearances*, not underlying objects: it doesn't count fingers, it renders hand-*ish* regions the way hands usually look, and small errors in count aren't visible to its process. Letters are the same: it learned what writing *looks like* — the texture of text — without the spelling being load-bearing, so signs come out as convincing gibberish. And its sense of what things look like is an imprint of its training images, biases included. So the honest summary: the image is genuinely created, from noise, by a process that knows the look of things far better than the logic of things — which is exactly the profile of its triumphs and its tells.
